rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Elmalılı says gāsık can describe something filling, darkening, flowing, pouring, cold, or otherwise marked by gasak.
rows.anchor: dolan, kararan, karanlık eden, akan, dökülen, domlu, posarık, soğuk olan

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Waqab first denotes entering a hollow, then more broadly entering, disappearing, arriving, darkness setting in, sunset, or lunar eclipse; entry suits all proposed meanings of gāsık.
rows.anchor: masdar olarak “vakb”, “vukūb” da çukura girmek demek olup sonra mutlaka girmek

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The most common reading takes gāsık as night and waqab as night darkness spreading over everything, yielding refuge from a night’s evil when darkness falls.
rows.anchor: karanlığı bastığı vakit bir gecenin şerrinden” demek olur

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Night is associated with its evil as the time when it occurs; this is a figurative attribution like calling a day fasting, meaning evil occurring at night.
rows.anchor: şerrin geceye izâfeti hudûsuna zarf olması hasebiyle mülâbisine izâfet kabîlindendir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Specifying the onset of darkness warns that evil begins spreading then, so protection through seeking refuge must be secured before it takes hold.
rows.anchor: şerrin o zaman yayılmaya başlaması ve binâen‘aleyh şer istîlâ etmeden önce isti‘âze

rows.speaker: İbn Abbas ve Mücâhid
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and Mujahid are reported to interpret gāsık as night and waqab as darkness entering and spreading.
rows.anchor: “Gāsık”ın böyle leyl ile ve “vukūb”un duhûl-i zalâm ile tefsîrini

rows.speaker: Dahhâk ve Hasan
rows.claim: Dahhak is also cited for the night interpretation, and Hasan is said to have transmitted it.
rows.anchor: Dahhâk’ten tahric eylemişler, Hasan’dan da rivayet olunmuştur

rows.speaker: Zeccâc
rows.claim: Zajjaj interprets gāsık as cold and applies it to night because night is colder than day.
rows.anchor: Zeccâc da buna zâhib olmuş, ancak “gāsıkı” bârid

rows.speaker: Râgıb
rows.claim: Raghib says gasak is intense darkness and gāsık is night, whose evil is a sudden nocturnal misfortune, like a night visitor.
rows.anchor: Râgıb “gasak”ın şiddet-i zulmet, “gāsık”ın gece mânasına olduğunu söylemiş

rows.speaker: Zemahşerî
rows.claim: Zamakhshari derives night’s darkness from filling or thickening, like an eye filling with tears or a wound with blood.
rows.anchor: Zemahşerî de “gasak-ı leyl”in aslı gözün yaşla, yaranın kanla dolması gibi imtilâ mânasına

rows.speaker: Hazret-i Âişe
rows.claim: Aisha reports that the Prophet pointed to the moon and told her to seek God’s protection from its evil, identifying it as gāsık when it waqab.
rows.anchor: Hazret-i Âişe’den şöyle rivayet etmişlerdir, demiştir ki: “Bir gün Resûlullah sallallâhu aleyhi ve sellem Kamer’e baktı

rows.speaker: Tirmizî
rows.claim: Tirmidhi grades the report in which the Prophet identifies the moon as gāsık when it waqab as hasan sahih.
rows.anchor: Tirmizî demiştir ki: “Bu hadis, hasen sahihtir.”

rows.speaker: Âlûsî
rows.claim: Alusi argues that anyone accepting the moon report’s authenticity should not turn to another interpretation.
rows.anchor: Âlûsî “bunun sıhhatini teslim eyleyenin diğer bir tefsire udûl etmemesi gerektir” demiş

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Elmalılı rejects the claim that the authentic moon report requires restricting the verse to one interpretation; one report need not narrow the word’s apparent generality.
rows.anchor: buna kasrın lüzûmunu men‘ile cevap verilebilir. Zira, Kamer’in gāsık olmasının sıhhati teslim olunur

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation calls the moon gāsık because it is full of light at the full moon; waqab then means its darkening in eclipse.
rows.anchor: Birincisi: Bedir hâlinde nûr ile dolgunluğu itibariyledir, bu surette vukūbu husûfa dâhil olup kararmasıdır

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second explanation links the moon to flowing movement and speed as it traverses the zodiac; gasak is borrowed from flowing or running.
rows.anchor: İkincisi: Seyr ü hareketinde, burûcu kat‘ında sür‘ati itibariyledir ki “gask” seyelândan cereyâna müste‘âr olur

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third explanation says the moon’s light is borrowed from the sun while its body is dark, so waqab is its disappearance at eclipse or the end of the month.
rows.anchor: cirmi haddizâtında muzlim olması itibariyledir. Bu iki vecihte vukūbu şehrin âhirinde mihâka girerek gāib olmasıdır

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Astrologers deem eclipse and new-moon times inauspicious, and sorcerers are said to work then; linking the verse’s occasion to magic was therefore called apt.
rows.anchor: Müneccimler husûf ve mihâk zamanını nahs sayarlar, sâhirler de marazı mûris sihir ile o zaman iştigal ederler

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Elmalılı rejects restricting the evil to sorcery at eclipse or new moon, since that accommodates astrologers’ and magicians’ assumptions and revives superstitions the Prophet rejected.
rows.anchor: müneccimlerin, sâhirlerin zu‘mlarına göre bir nevi mümâşâtı tazammun edeceğinden dolayı münâsib olmadığı gibi

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The moon’s evil at eclipse or new moon is darkness prevailing as its light disappears, returning the interpretation to the general evil of night.
rows.anchor: Doğrusu Kamer’in husûf veya mihâkı zamanında şerrinin mânası da nûrun gaybûbetiyle zulmetin istîlâsındaki şer demek

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The moon’s waqab can include setting, but the full moon sets near dawn, when night’s darkness is not taking hold; hence interpreters especially specify eclipse or the moon’s final nights.
rows.anchor: bedir hâlindeki dolgun Kamer’in gurûbunu sabah tâkip edeceği için bunda gecenin vukūbu zamanı tahakkuk eylemez

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aisha’s report can mean moonlit nights are not gāsık; the dark night is gāsık only when the moon waqab, confirming night or darkness without requiring a restrictive reading.
rows.anchor: mehtab gecelerinin gāsık olmadığını, gecenin gāsık olması, Kamer’in vukūbu zamanına maksur bulunduğunu îzah etmek

rows.speaker: İbn Şihab
rows.claim: Ibn Shihab interprets gāsık when waqab as the sun at sunset; the ensuing disappearance of twilight marks the entry of night darkness.
rows.anchor: İbn Ebî Hâtim’in İbn Şihab’dan tahrîcine göre غَاسِقٍ إِذَا وَقَبَ gurûb ettiği vakit Şems’tir

rows.speaker: İbn Zeyd
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says Arabs called the setting of the Pleiades gāsık; illness and plague increased during its setting and receded when it rose.
rows.anchor: İbn Zeyd demiştir ki: “Araplar ‘gāsık Süreyyâ’nın sukūtudur’ derlerdi ve onun sukūtu sırasında emrâz ve tâun çok olur

rows.speaker: Resûlullah
rows.claim: A report from Abu Hurayra attributed to the Prophet identifies the dark gāsık as a star, supporting the Pleiades interpretation.
rows.anchor: Ebû Hüreyre’den Hazret-i Peygamber’e merfû‘an rivayet olunmuştur: “‘وَمِن شَرِّ غَاسِقٍ إِذَا وَقَبَ en-necmi’l-gāsık’ buyurdu”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Elmalılı notes that al-najm means the Pleiades and cites a report that calamities recede when it rises; some versions specify the Arabian Peninsula.
rows.anchor: mâlum ki “en-Necm” Süreyyâ demektir, bundan başka Ve’n-Necmi sûresinde de geçtiği vechile

rows.speaker: Âlûsî
rows.claim: Alusi points to further versions in Munawi’s commentary on Jami al-Saghir; even here, the sense can revert to dark nights when the Pleiades is absent.
rows.anchor: Âlûsî der ki: “Câmi‘u’s-Sağīr’in Münâvî şerh-i kebîrinde diğer rivayetler de vardır

rows.speaker: Sâhib-Keşşâf
rows.claim: The author of al-Kashshaf allows gāsık to mean a black snake and waqab its bite.
rows.anchor: Sâhib-Keşşâf der ki: “Gāsık ile kara yılan, ve vukūbu sokması murad olunmak dahi câizdir.”

rows.speaker: Kāmûs sâhibi
rows.claim: A lexicon quotation gives gāsık as the groin swelling with lust and waqab as its attack.
rows.anchor: Kāmûs sâhibinin “vakb” maddesinde bir nakline göre “gāsık”, ihtiras ile dolup kabaran kasık

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Elmalılı does not rely on these two interpretations, but says the snake exemplifies a dangerous enemy and lust or greed can be major sources of evil worth seeking refuge from.
rows.anchor: Bu iki mâna mu‘avvel görülmezse de yılan sakınılması lâzım gelen en muzır düşmanlardan olmakta mesel olduğu gibi

rows.speaker: Âlûsî
rows.claim: Alusi questions the attribution in al-Qamus, which reports a sense from Ghazali and others on Ibn Abbas’s authority.
rows.anchor: Âlûsî der ki: “Fîrûzâbâdî Kāmûs’ta

rows.speaker: Râzî
rows.claim: Razi transmits a mystical hierarchy: elemental bodies subject to generation and decay contain evils, while ethereal bodies are wholly good and free of defect.
rows.anchor: Râzî’nin “bazı ârifînden işittim” diye nakleylediği mânadır. Bu iki sûrede mahlûkātın merâtibi şerhedildiğini

rows.speaker: Râzî
rows.claim: In the mystical account, solid matter lacks psychic powers and is pure darkness; it represents gāsık when it waqab.
rows.anchor: Cemâdât, kuvâyı nefsâniyenin hepsinden hâlîdirler, onun için bunlarda zulmet hâlis, envâr bi’l-külliye zâildir

rows.speaker: Râzî
rows.claim: The same account figures plant growth in length, breadth, and depth as a force blowing on three knots.
rows.anchor: Nebâtât ise kuvve-i gāziye-i nebâtiye tûl, arz, umkta nemalanıp artandır, onun için bu kuvve-i nâmiye

rows.speaker: Râzî
rows.claim: It says animal senses, desire, and anger distract the human spirit from the unseen and divine holiness, and interprets the next verse’s envier as these powers.
rows.anchor: kuvâ-yı hayvâniye havâss-ı zâhire ve havâss-ı bâtıne ve şehvet ve gazabdır

rows.speaker: Râzî
rows.claim: This interpretation sees the human soul’s further ranks as the subject of the following Sura al-Nas.
rows.anchor: merâtibi de bundan sonra Sûre-i Nâs’ta zikrolunmuştur

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Elmalılı explains that the mystical account takes gāsık as darkness or blackness and identifies it with inert elemental matter, pure passivity.
rows.anchor: bunda “gāsık” muzlim, karaltı mânasına olarak ecsâm-ı unsuriyeden hiç kuvve-i nâmiye

rows.speaker: İbn Sînâ
rows.claim: Avicenna instead interprets gāsık as the animal faculty, a turbid dark force opposed to the rational soul, which is pure by nature but becomes sullied by animality.
rows.anchor: İbn Sînâ da bu mâna üzerinde yürümüş, fakat “gāsık”ı sırf cism-i

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Elmalılı prefers reading gāsık broadly as elemental matter, then specifying plants and animals or desire and anger, following the verses’ movement from general to particular.
rows.anchor: bunu ne sade cism-i câmid kısmına ne de kuvve-i hayvâniyeye tahsis etmeyip nebâtât ve hayvânâta şâmil olacak vechile mutlak cism-i unsurî diye ahzetmek

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This broad reading covers evil in the dark material world under generation and decay, including bodily dark forces or apparitions that descend upon a person and the failing mortal body’s end and bad death.
rows.anchor: bütün şerlere şâmil olacağı cihetle, insanın karşısında ahz-ı mevki‘ederek üzerine dalan cismânî herhangi bir kara kuvvetin veya hayâletin âfetini iş‘ar edeceği gibi

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation treats gāsık as any dark calamity causing pain, distress, or obstruction, a material or spiritual evil described as darkness; waqab means attack.
rows.anchor: herhangi bir kara musibet demek olduğu da söylenmiştir ki, insanın vicdânına

rows.speaker: İbn Cerîr
rows.claim: Ibn Jarir prefers the broadest view: gāsık is anything dark, and refuge is sought from the evil of each such thing when it enters or appears, since God did not specify one referent.
rows.anchor: Allah teâlâ bunların hiçbirini tahsis etmemiş, ta‘mîm eylemiştir, o hâlde ‘gāsık’ denilebilenin her birinin de vukūbu zamanındaki şerrinden isti‘âze

rows.speaker: Katâde
rows.claim: Qatada glosses waqab with ذهب, ‘went away’; Ibn Jarir includes the gloss while explaining the night’s entry into darkness.
rows.anchor: Katâde وَقَبَ’ın mânasında ذهب der idi

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Elmalılı renders the phrase as seeking refuge from those blowing into knots, including cord knots, knots of resolve or belief, and sorcerous spells made in an obscure manner by witches, women, or groups.
rows.anchor: Meâl: ve o, ukdelere üfleyen nefeslerin şerrinden

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author of al-Kashshaf says nafs is a puff with saliva.
rows.anchor: Sâhib-Keşşâf “tükürükle nefhdir” demiş

rows.speaker: Sâhib-Levâmih
rows.claim: Al-Lawamih says ruqya can be performed by a breath-like puff without saliva, while a puff with saliva is called tafl.
rows.anchor: Sâhib-Levâmih[^3] de “nefhe benzer tükürüksüz olarak rukye de yapılır

rows.speaker: İbn Kayyim
rows.claim: Ibn Qayyim says sorcerers use foul breath mixed with some of their ingredients to enlist the effects of their acts; Alusi therefore considers al-Kashshaf’s saliva view more accurate.
rows.anchor: İbn Kayyim de: “Sâhirler sihir yaptıkları zaman fiillerinin tesirine habis nefeslerinin bazı eczâsı karışan bir nefesle isti‘âne ederler”

rows.speaker: Râgıb
rows.claim: Raghib distinguishes nafs as emitting saliva less than tafl, applies it to a healer’s or sorcerer’s breath into knots, and compares it to a snake expelling venom.
rows.anchor: Fi’l-vâki‘Râgıb da der ki: “‘Nefs’ tükrük fırlatmaktır

rows.speaker: Nihâye
rows.claim: Al-Nihaya says nafs resembles breath and is less than tafl, since tafl always includes some saliva; this implies saliva is not required for nafs.
rows.anchor: Nihâye’de, ‘nefs’ ‘nefh’e şebîhtir ve tefl’den ekaldir, çünkü tefl her hâlde tükrükten bir şey karışmadan olmaz

rows.speaker: Kāmûs sâhibi
rows.claim: The lexicon likewise equates nafs with breath and distinguishes it from tafl, which is a puff with a little saliva; its translator describes the distinction.
rows.anchor: Kāmûs sâhibi de böyle “nefs, nefh gibidir ve teflden ekaldir” demiş

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Elmalılı concludes that nafs can be a simple breath without saliva, as in familiar recitation and healing, though sorcerers may spit venomously as snakes do.
rows.anchor: “nefs”in esasında biraz tükürük fırlatmak olsa bile “nefh” gibi tükürüksüz sade nefes etmekle de olur

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nafkh can also mean giving life or imparting spirit, and nafs can figuratively mean the Holy Spirit casting meaning, knowledge, or speech into the heart; therefore there are holy as well as foul breaths.
rows.anchor: Rûhu’l-Kudüs kalbime nefs (نفث) eyledi” ilh...”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse concerns foul breaths whose harm is sought against, especially the familiar venomous spells of sorcerers, which made the phrase a name for them.
rows.anchor: burada mevzû‘-i bahis, şerrinden isti‘âze

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An-naffathat fi al-uqad can be parsed as a locative adverbial or as a settled adverbial functioning as their state.
rows.anchor: “ٱلنَّفَّٰثَٰتِ,”فِى ٱلْعُقَدِ’ın zarfı veya zarf-ı müstekar olarak onların hâlidir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Uqda is the plural of knot, from tying ends firmly together, but because akd applies to tangible and intangible bonds, uqda has many related senses beyond a cord knot.
rows.anchor: “Ukde” bir şeyin uçlarını derleyip birbirine sıkı tutturmak, yani düğüm bağlamak

rows.speaker: Kāmûs
rows.claim: Al-Qamus lists uqda as a knot or knot-place and also uses it for authority over towns, allegiance to rulers, property, and tangled or abundant places and resources.
rows.anchor: 1. Ukde, düğüm ve düğüm yeri,

rows.speaker: Nihâye
rows.claim: Al-Nihaya explains the hadith about the people of the knot as those holding authority over provincial towns, from the banner bound for commanders.
rows.anchor: Hazret-i Ömer hadîsinde هَلَكَ أَهْلُ الْعَقْدِ وَرَبِّ الْكَعْبَةِ ‘emsâr üzerine velâyet ashâbı helâk oldu’ demektir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lexical senses also include a person’s livelihood or support, abundance, required or certain obligations such as marriage and sale, and the firmness of a belief, attachment, resolve, or judgment.
rows.anchor: Herhangi bir şeyin vücûbu, kat‘iyyeti, lüzûmu ki ukde-i nikâh, bey‘vesâire bundandır

rows.speaker: Nihâye
rows.claim: Al-Nihaya reads the hadith’s ‘knot of regret’ as a firm resolve to repent, and the traveler’s refusal to untie a knot as not breaking his resolve before reaching Medina.
rows.anchor: sana kalblerimizden ukde-i nedem’, nedâmete akd-i azim demektir ki tevbeyi tahkiktir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Uqda can also denote anger, a reed, or a place-name; these senses branch from its underlying idea of a knot.
rows.anchor: Kin ve gazaba da cemi‘sîgasıyla “ukad” denir, تَحَلَّلَتْ عُقَدُهُ “düğümleri çözüldü”

rows.speaker: Râgıb
rows.claim: Raghib says akd first applies to physical cords or buildings, then metaphorically to contracts and covenants; uqda names what is bound, including marriage, oath, or stammering speech.
rows.anchor: “akd”in evvelâ “akd-i habl” ve “akd-i binâ” gibi ecsâm-ı sulbede kullanıldığını, sonra da akd-i bey‘, ahd ve sâire gibi me‘ânîye istiare edildiğini

rows.speaker: Râgıb
rows.claim: Raghib interprets the sorceress’s knots as spells rooted in resolve, which is why both the witch and the spell may be described through binding language.
rows.anchor: ٱلنَّفَّٰثَٰتِ فِى ٱلْعُقَدِ’da ‘ukde’nin cem‘idir, ve bu sâhirenin akdettiğidir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A sorcerer’s knots are resolve-knots: their ends are first tied within the sorcerers themselves, through which they seek to impose their will on others by devilish means.
rows.anchor: sâhirin, sâhirenin üflediği, akdettiği ukdeler, düğümlediği düğümler bu mânalarla alâkadar bir azm ve azîmet düğümüdür

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Azm or azima is the heart’s firm commitment and directed intention to carry out an act, also described as striving and persevering with seriousness.
rows.anchor: “azm” ve “azîmet” bir işin icrâsına akd-i kalbdir, yani kat‘î rabt-ı kalb ile kasd ü teveccüh kılmaktır

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Azima names major good works and essential duties that must be carried out without seeking a concession.
rows.anchor: büyük hayırlı işlere ve ruhsat ciheti aranmayarak icrâsı matlub olan

rows.speaker: Râgıb
rows.claim: Raghib describes a sorcerer’s resolve as a spell of protection that imaginatively binds the devil to execute the sorcerer’s will.
rows.anchor: Râgıb bunu şöyle târif etmiştir: “O azîmet bir ta‘vîz, yani bir sığındırma efsunudur

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Blowing into knots can be understood physically or figuratively as directing breath, speech, or suggestion toward forming or undoing bonds and stirring people’s minds.
rows.anchor: nefes sarf eylemek ilkāât ve telkīnât ile nefisler üzerinde tehyîcât ve tahrîkâtta bulunmak

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since the passage concerns evil souls, its clearest example is sorcerers’ devilish, deliberate blowing or spitting to bind and control others through spells.
rows.anchor: işleri güçleri küfr ü fitne olan sâhirlerin efsun düğümleriyle şunu bunu bağlamak, teshir etmek için

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The feminine plural naffathat has three proposed feminine referents: women, souls, or groups.
rows.anchor: bunun müennes olan mevsûfunu takdirde üç vecih söylenmiştir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first reading supplies women: witchcraft is commonly associated with women, and women’s guile or charm is said to exert a bewitching influence even for those who deny magic.
rows.anchor: Birisi, bâlâda işaret olunduğu üzere cadılık ekseriyetle kadınların şi‘ârı olması

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second reading supplies souls, grammatically feminine in Arabic and applicable to men and women, individuals and communities, making it the broadest and most preferred interpretation and the one adopted in the translation.
rows.anchor: Bu mâna erkeğe ve dişiye ferdlere ve cemiyetlere sâdık olmak itibariyle daha şümullü olduğu

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third reading supplies groups, since collective sorcery is more severe; it includes men and women but does not clearly cover individuals.
rows.anchor: Çünkü sâhirlerin ictimâ‘ıyla yapılan sihir daha eşeddir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The widely accepted interpretation is female or collective sorcerers who tie knots in thread and blow spells over them.
rows.anchor: İpliklere düğümler döğüp de onlara üfleyerek rukye ve efsun yapan sâhire karıların veya nefislerin veya cemaatlerin şerrinden

rows.speaker: İbn Abbas
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas explains the phrase as ruqyas mixed with sorcery.
rows.anchor: Muhammed b. Sa‘d tarîkiyle İbn Abbas’tan: وَمِن شَرِّ ٱلنَّفَّٰثَٰتِ فِى ٱلْعُقَدِ sihir karışan rukyeler

rows.speaker: Hasan
rows.claim: Hasan interprets the phrase as sorceresses and sorcerers.
rows.anchor: Hasan’dan: Sevâhir ve sehara

rows.speaker: Katâde
rows.claim: Qatada recited the verse and warned people to avoid ruqyas mixed with sorcery.
rows.anchor: Katâde’den: وَمِن شَرِّ ٱلنَّفَّٰثَٰتِ فِى ٱلْعُقَدِ okumuş ve “şu rukyelerin sihir karışanından sakınınız” demiştir

rows.speaker: Tâvus
rows.claim: Tawus says no ruqya is closer to shirk than the ruqya of the possessed.
rows.anchor: Tâvus’tan: “Rukye-i mecânîn”den daha ziyade şirke

rows.speaker: Mücâhid ve İkrime
rows.claim: Mujahid and Ikrima interpret the phrase as ruqyas performed over thread-knots.
rows.anchor: Mücâhid ve İkrime de demiştir ki: ٱلنَّفَّٰثَٰتِ فِى ٱلْعُقَدِ “İplik ukdelerinde rukyelerdir.”

rows.speaker: İkrime
rows.claim: Ikrima identifies the thread-knot practice as binding, called ahza in Arabic.
rows.anchor: İkrime demiştir ki iplik ukdelerinde ahzdır, (yani “bağlama” tâbir olunan tutukluktur

rows.speaker: İbn Zeyd
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd interprets the blowers as sorceresses working among knots.
rows.anchor: İbn Zeyd’den: ٱلنَّفَّٰثَٰتِ ukdelerde sâhirelerdir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Only Mujahid and Ikrima specifically restrict the knots to thread knots; this distinction shows that sincere healing recitation without sorcery may be permissible.
rows.anchor: iplik ukdesi ile tahsîsi ancak Mücâhid ve İkrime’den vârid olmuştur

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sincere prayer or Qur’an recitation for healing is not harmful deception or appeal to other than God; these suras command seeking refuge in God from every evil.
rows.anchor: hulûs-i kalb ve niyyet-i salâh

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet recited over himself and others and permitted beneficial ruqya, which is reported to have healed spiritual and bodily illness; the verse also warns against sorcerers and magic-mixed treatments.
rows.anchor: Resûlullah’ın kendisine ve diğerlerine bu suretle okuyup üflediği ve böyle hayır için rukyeye müsaade eylediği sâbit

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some jurists prohibit treatment by recitation, citing reports that certain servants avoid cautery and requested ruqya and that one who seeks these treatments has not relied on God.
rows.anchor: Bazıları rukyeyi, yani okuma ile tedaviyi [6389] men‘eylemişler, şu hadis ile istidlâl etmişlerdir

rows.speaker: Sa‘îd b. Cübeyr
rows.claim: Sa‘id questions Husayn for requesting ruqya after a sting, invoking a report that ruqya is only for the evil eye or a venomous bite.
rows.anchor: ‘Seni ona ne sevketti?’ dedi, ‘Şa‘bî’nin bize tahdis ettiği bir hadis’ dedim

rows.speaker: Hazret-i Peygamber
rows.claim: The Prophet describes seventy thousand who enter Paradise without reckoning as those who do not perform or request ruqya, avoid omens, and trust their Lord.
rows.anchor: هُمُ الَّذِينَ لاَ يـَرْقُونَ وَلاَ يَسْتـَرْقُونَ وَلاَ يـَتَطَيـَّرُونَ وَعَلَى رَبِّهِمْ يـَتـَوَكَّلُونَ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Elmalılı says this concerns people of the highest trust who avoid reliance on causes; it does not justify a general prohibition, and a more authentic version omits ‘they do not perform ruqya.’
rows.anchor: Bu daha sahihtir. Bu hadis, İhlâs’ta “samed”in mânasını îzahta geçtiği üzere esbâba gönül vermeyen

rows.speaker: Câbir b. Abdullah
rows.claim: Jabir reports that the Prophet first forbade ruqya, then told those able to benefit a brother to do so after Jabir’s uncle sought permission to treat scorpion stings.
rows.anchor: Câbir b. Abdullah hadislerinde demiştir ki: “Benim bir dayım vardı, akrepten rukye ederdi

rows.speaker: Avf b. Mâlik Eşca‘î
rows.claim: Awf reports that the Prophet permitted ruqyas after hearing them, provided they contain no shirk.
rows.anchor: Avf b. Mâlik Eşca‘î hadîsinde de demiştir ki: “Biz câhiliyede rukye ederdik

rows.speaker: Ebû Sa‘îd-i Hudrî
rows.claim: Abu Sa‘id recounts reciting al-Fatiha for a tribe’s snake-bitten chief, who recovered; the Prophet approved the healing and allowed them to accept a flock as payment.
rows.anchor: Ashab içinden bir recül -ki Ebû Sa‘îd kendisidir- ‘evet’ dedi, vardı onu Fâtihatü’l-Kitâb ile rukye etti

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These reports show that the prohibited ruqyas are those with unknown content, possible sorcery, or shirk.
rows.anchor: nehyedilmiş olan rukyeler hakikatleri mechul olan, sihir ihtimâli ve şirk mânası bulunan rukyelerdir

rows.speaker: İkrime
rows.claim: Ikrima says a healer should neither blow, wipe, nor tie knots during ruqya.
rows.anchor: İkrime demiştir ki: “Rukye eden üflememeli ve meshetmemeli

rows.speaker: İbrâhim-i Neha‘î
rows.claim: Ibrahim al-Nakha‘i reports that the early Muslims disliked blowing during ruqya.
rows.anchor: İbrâhim-i Neha‘î’den de “selef rukyelerde üflemeyi mekruh görürlerdi” diye menkuldür

rows.speaker: Dahhâk
rows.claim: In an anecdote, Dahhak permits reciting a protective charm over his pain but asks the visitor not to blow; the visitor recites the two refuge suras.
rows.anchor: ‘Sana ta‘vîz okuyayım mı yâ Ebâ Muhammed?’ dedim, ‘peki, velâkin üfleme’ dedi

rows.speaker: Halîmî
rows.claim: Halimi says Ikrima’s rationale is weak: harmful sorcery is blameworthy, but breath intended to heal body or spirit is not forbidden.
rows.anchor: fakat bu istidlâl zayıftır çünkü نفث في العقد ancak ervâh ve ebdâna muzır sihir olduğu vakit mezmum olur

rows.speaker: Resûlullah
rows.claim: A report from Abu Hurayra says whoever ties a knot and blows into it has practiced sorcery, sorcery is shirk, and whoever attaches himself to an object is left to it.
rows.anchor: Nesâî’de Ebû Hüreyre’den şu hadis de mervîdir: Resûlullah sallallâhu aleyhi ve sellem buyurdu ki

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Elmalılı explains that relying on an amulet or object instead of God brings no benefit and deprives the person of divine help; the hadith targets magical knot-spells, not every healing breath.
rows.anchor: yalnız Allah’a sığınmayıp da o şeye bağlandığı, ondan umduğu, hâlbuki Allah’ın izni olmayınca hiçbir şeyin ne menfaati ne mazarratı olamayacağı

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning concerns obscure or doubtful sorcery and credulity; most exegetes focus on magic-mixed ruqya, while some regarded even blowing or touching as suspect.
rows.anchor: müfessirînin çoğu mânayı hep sihir üzerinde dolaştırmışlar ve mutlaka değil, fakat sihir karışan rukyelerden sakınmayı söylemişler

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: There are also holy, merciful breaths, and ordinary means can connect spiritual and material healing; treatment is legitimate when efficacy is attributed to God and fraud, sorcery, deception, and harm are avoided.
rows.anchor: tesir, esbâbdan değil, Allah’tan bilinmeli ve hepsinde de entrikadan, sihirbazlıktan, şarlatanlıktan

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Spiritual and bodily illnesses may be treated through spiritual, physical, or combined means, while good intention and sound belief matter even in bodily medicine.
rows.anchor: emrâz-ı rûhiyeye rûhânî, emrâz-ı cismâniyeye cismânî sebeplerle tedavi meşrû‘olduğu gibi

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Elmalılı warns that self-serving medical charlatans who prioritize fees can harm as much as occult practitioners, and he includes them among those blowing evil knots.
rows.anchor: Böylelerin de وَمِن شَرِّ ٱلنَّفَّٰثَٰتِ فِى ٱلْعُقَدِ’de dâhil efsunculardan sayılması lâzım gelir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: By the broad senses of uqda, anyone in any trade who spends breath to deceive people or spread evil belongs among the harmful souls from whom refuge is sought; this does not deny the worth of those serving truth and good.
rows.anchor: her meslek ve san‘atta hak ve hayır fikrinden ayrılarak insan aldatmak, şer saçmak için nefes sarfedenlerin hepsi de bu mazmunda dâhil

rows.speaker: Cibrîl
rows.claim: A report says Gabriel recited over the Prophet during illness, seeking God’s protection from whatever harmed him and asking God to heal him.
rows.anchor: Resûlullah sallallâhu aleyhi ve sellem bir rahatsız olmuştu. Cibrîl aleyhisselâm ona rukye etti

rows.speaker: İbn Abbas
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the Prophet taught a prayer for every pain and fever, seeking refuge in God from the harm of a throbbing vein and the heat of fire.
rows.anchor: İbn Abbas demiştir ki: “Resûlullah sallallâhu aleyhi ve sellem bize bütün evcâ‘dan

rows.speaker: Resûlullah
rows.claim: The Prophet taught that whoever asks the Lord of the Mighty Throne seven times to heal a sick person whose time has not come will see that person healed.
rows.anchor: Bir kimse eceli gelmemiş bir hastanın yanına girer de yedi kere

rows.speaker: Resûlullah
rows.claim: When visiting the sick, the Prophet prayed that the Lord of people remove the illness and heal, since only God’s healing leaves no sickness.
rows.anchor: Resûlullah sallallâhu aleyhi ve sellem bir hastanın yanına girdiğinde şöyle derdi

rows.speaker: Resûlullah
rows.claim: The Prophet sought protection for Hasan and Husayn in God’s perfect words from every devil, harmful creature, and evil eye, and said Abraham did likewise for Ismail and Isaac.
rows.anchor: Resûlullah sallallâhu aleyhi ve sellem Hazret-i Hasan ile Hazret-i Hüseyin’e ta‘vîz eder

rows.speaker: Osman b. Ebi’l-Âs-ı Sekafî
rows.claim: Uthman reports that the Prophet instructed him to place his hand on pain and repeat a prayer seeking refuge in God’s might and power; he recovered after doing so.
rows.anchor: Osman b. Ebi’l-Âs-ı Sekafî’den; demiştir ki: “Resûlullah’a vardım ve bende bir veca‘vardı

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Elmalılı notes that the Prophet did not recite over Uthman but instructed Uthman to recite for himself.
rows.anchor: Bunda şâyân-ı dikkattir ki Resûlullah ona okumamış, onun kendisine okutmuştur
